items.title: Glutamine's three mechanism sentences
items.where: Some Causes of poor gut health, P20
items.your_version:
Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation is what you get when there's not enough of the fuels each type of cell in your gut prefers (glutamine and butyrate). Your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, to keep its tight junctions intact. If the cells lining your small intestine (called enterocytes) or the colonocytes lining your large intestine don't get that energy, the barrier loosens up. Then lipopolysaccharides (LPS, which come from the walls of bacteria) and other endotoxins leak through those (not-so-tight)-junction gaps into your bloodstream.
L-Glutamine (watch Dr. Rhonda vid) is the main fuel for your enterocytes, and for your immune cells when they're activated. It doesn't have to go through the complicated digestive steps other nutrients do. Inside the mitochondria, it gets converted into alpha-ketoglutarate, or α-KG, which then goes into the citric acid cycle, which is how the mitochondria make their energy. So that's why consuming pure glutamine gives energy to those cells faster than eating food. They then use their extra energy to repair the gut lining by pulling the tight junctions together, and that keeps LPS from getting through. Glutamine also provides nitrogen to help build new cells.
Take 5g a day as a baseline. The point of that baseline is to counter the breakdown of the gut lining that high-intensity or high-volume training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.
CAUTION: cancer cells also love glutamine as a fuel, especially fast-growing cancers. Special caution is needed with intestinal or liver cancers, because glutamine is trapped by the intestines, but it goes to the liver along with the blood that takes nutrients to the liver from your gut via the portal vein.

items.title: The 5g baseline: who it's for, and why training
items.where: Some Causes of poor gut health, P21
items.comment: incorporate your research to make this more accurate and useful pls, this article is from research i did last year, with gemini and some books and vids
items.my_version: Take 5g a day as a baseline, to keep your enterocytes fed. The 5g also counters the breakdown of the gut lining that hard or long training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. While you train, your body sends blood away from your gut to your working muscles, so your enterocytes get less oxygen and fuel. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.

items.title: The glutamine caution, for any active cancer
items.where: Some Causes of poor gut health, P22
items.my_version: CAUTION: a lot of cancers feed on glutamine too, to fuel their growth. Your enterocytes take in a lot of it as soon as it reaches them, but not all of it, and the rest gets into your blood, where a cancer can get to it. They can only take in so much at a time, so the bigger the dose, the more of it gets into your blood. So if you have an active cancer, check with your oncologist before you take the 5g, and especially before you go up to the 10-30g.
items.before: CAUTION: cancer cells that multiply really fast can grab glutamine too, to fuel their growth. So if you have an active colon or liver cancer, don't raise the dose that high. The liver is on that list because the blood from your gut goes straight there, through the portal vein, so a big dose of glutamine reaches your liver before anywhere else.
